editions.title: Iran strikes spread as Nvidia's Huang fallout and Xi-Putin-Trump summit loom
editions.notification: US-Iran strikes enter a seventh night, Nvidia's leadership crisis deepens, and a first Xi-Putin-Trump summit is set.
editions.intro:
The conflict with Iran is the lead story again, now in its seventh consecutive night of strikes. Iranian missiles and drones have targeted US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait, and reports say at least five people died in a strike on a wedding in Kuhestak. Kuwait suspended operations at its international airport, and Iran's energy ministry asked citizens to cut power use after strikes on the grid. Separately, reports say the Trump administration warned Gulf allies that hostilities could resume as soon as Wednesday. Figures from both sides are unverified, and the White House has not confirmed any timing.

The second thread is Nvidia. Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive, after reports of affairs including one with a Singapore-based executive US officials say was recruited by Chinese intelligence, has wiped roughly $600bn from the company's value in a week. Colette Kress is interim chief executive, and the first results without Huang are due on 17 November. Lawmakers are pressing for testimony, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under scrutiny, and Huang reportedly discussed a return. Bessent has called for a "dramatic shakeup".

Diplomacy and markets are tied to both. A first in-person Xi-Trump-Putin meeting is set for Shenzhen during APEC, with nuclear arms on the agenda. Anthropic's IPO, priced at up to $1.4tn, is due to price on 18 November. Oil is elevated, with Brent near $94 to $96, and the Fed is signalling possible rate rises, which pushed the dollar to a 19-month high.

editions.title: Nvidia's Huang fallout deepens as Iran strikes widen
editions.notification: Huang's exit is rattling Nvidia and Congress, while US-Iran strikes enter a seventh night. Here's where things stand.
editions.intro:
Nvidia remains the day's dominant story, though the focus has shifted from Jensen Huang's resignation to what happens next. Huang has reportedly agreed to testify before Congress, with Senate and House committees seeking closed-door interviews on 1 to 3 December. Pressure is building on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is accused of stalling action against Megaspeed, the Singapore firm linked to Alice Huang. Nvidia has lost roughly $550bn in five days, and its first results without Huang are due on 17 November. A petition with more than 115,000 signatures, including Elon Musk, now asks the board to reinstate him.

The biggest geopolitical story is the widening US-Iran conflict. A seventh consecutive night of American strikes has prompted Iranian missile and drone attacks on US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait, with reports of civilian deaths in Kuhestak. Two oil tankers were reportedly hit by mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and crude prices rose. Diplomacy is also moving: the White House confirmed a trilateral meeting of Trump, Xi and Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 19 November, though no agreement is expected and Ukraine is not on the agenda. Europe has chosen five national security advisers to represent it in future talks, while Moscow's reported demands on Nato and Britain set a hard starting point.

Markets were under broader pressure. US Treasuries had their worst week since the 2025 tariff announcement after higher-than-expected inflation, and Fed officials signal rate rises. Bitcoin fell to a three-month low near $63,000, and Anthropic's Nasdaq listing, priced at up to about $1.4tn, is set for 18 November. FAA disruption from a copper-to-fibre upgrade failure left about 1.5 million travellers affected, with normal operations expected before Thanksgiving.

editions.notification: Nvidia shares slide after Jensen Huang quits as CEO; Colette Kress steps in as interim chief.
editions.intro:
Nvidia dominated the day after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive, president and board member following reports of extramarital affairs, one reportedly involving a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The shares closed down just over 4% on Friday after falling as much as 14% in morning trading, and the stock has lost close to $1 trillion this month. Colette Kress is interim chief executive, Harvey Jones is the new independent chair, and the board has reportedly approached Arm's Rene Haas about the permanent role. The political fallout is spreading to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is accused of stalling action against Singapore's Megaspeed, and Democrats and Republicans are seeking answers.

Elsewhere, the White House confirmed that Donald Trump will meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, expected on 19 November, though a senior US official said no agreement is expected. Putin, meanwhile, signalled no compromise on Ukraine after meeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow. Europe agreed a five-nation group to speak for it in future talks.

Markets were also shaken by a global Microsoft 365 outage and a rare nationwide FAA ground stop that cancelled more than 6,700 US flights. On energy, the IEA says global oil supply has returned to surplus for the first time since the Iran war began, while Iran says two tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

editions.title: Nvidia's Huang out as CEO; Lutnick under fire
editions.notification: Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia CEO, wiping hundreds of billions off its value. Here is what it means for chips and Washington.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is Nvidia's leadership upheaval. Co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive and director with immediate effect, after admitting affairs with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence reportedly linked to China's Ministry of State Security, and with Nvidia vice-president Kimberly Powell. Colette Kress is interim chief executive and Harvey Jones is the first independent chair. Shares fell as much as 14% in early trading, and the company has lost up to $601 billion of value. The first results without Huang are due on 17 November.

The scandal is widening into US policy. Singapore has barred Alice Huang from re-entering the city-state, while saying US help in its Megaspeed probe was limited. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is reportedly under pressure from Congress and inside the White House after stalling export controls against Megaspeed, which CNN estimates bought more than $4bn of Nvidia chips. Commerce called reports of a clash with Treasury false. Trump has publicly backed Lutnick. Nvidia also privately told a lawmaker it could implement chip geotracking, which undercuts industry claims that such mandates are infeasible.

Beyond Nvidia, the day was dominated by fears for the AI trade. The Nasdaq fell more than 5% after Democrats' midterm gains raised the prospect of tougher AI and data-centre rules, wiping out over $2 trillion. Investors were not uniformly bearish: Nvidia largely recovered by Thursday's close, and Citi argued it is too early to call the AI trade structurally broken. OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue, though its losses widened, while Anthropic prepares its IPO next week.

editions.title: Jensen Huang quits Nvidia as CEO amid affair and China-spy scandal
editions.notification: Nvidia's Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO, wiping hundreds of billions off the chipmaker's value. Here's what it means.
editions.intro:
Nvidia's founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned with immediate effect, ending a 33-year run that made the chipmaker the most valuable in the world. The board named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive and Harvey Jones as its first independent chair. The exit follows reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence reportedly suspects of spying for China, and a second relationship with a direct report. Nvidia's shares fell as much as 14% in early trading, pushing market value below $4 trillion and erasing up to $601 billion, which would be the largest one-day loss for any stock if it held at the close.

The fallout is spreading into politics and markets. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have asked the administration to preserve records on Nvidia's China chip exports and on Huang's relationship, often a precursor to formal investigations. The New York Times reported that Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action, and the Wall Street Journal reported that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled action against Singapore-based Megaspeed, which may have funnelled chips to China. Trump has backed Lutnick publicly. Elsewhere, the tech sell-off hit broadly: the Nasdaq fell more than 5% on Thursday after Democrats' midterm gains raised fears of AI regulation and data-centre curbs.

The bigger question is what comes next. Nvidia reports quarterly results on 17 November, its first without Huang, and at least seven Wall Street firms have downgraded the stock this week. Anthropic's S-1 filing, which revealed rapid revenue growth and a claim that its models now run on AMD chips within days, adds pressure on Nvidia's software moat, while OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue. Investors will be watching the successor search and the governance fallout closely.

editions.title: Nvidia shares slide as reports of Jensen Huang's ouster mount
editions.notification: Nvidia shares tumble as reports say its board may move against CEO Jensen Huang. Here's what we know.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is Nvidia. Its shares fell more than 9.5 per cent over Monday and Tuesday and slid a further 7 to 8 per cent in after-hours trading on Wednesday, after the Wall Street Journal and New York Times reported that the board could meet as soon as the same day to decide the future of chief executive Jensen Huang. The reports follow Huang's admission of an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence agent, and a further alleged affair with Nvidia's vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell. Nvidia has hired former US attorney Joon H. Kim's firm to investigate, and US lawmakers have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing. Nvidia has not responded to comment requests, and the ouster reports remain unconfirmed rumours. Related chip stocks, including Korean memory makers and TSMC, are being watched for knock-on effects.

Elsewhere, the AI and chip economy kept generating deals. TSMC's board has reportedly approved up to $1 billion of investment in OpenAI and Anthropic, which would give the chipmaker direct stakes in two of its biggest customers, though analysts have flagged circular financing concerns. London chip designer Fractile raised $720 million at a $7 billion valuation, and South Korea's president said Samsung's packaging expansion could spur about $30 billion of further investment. Google DeepMind also unveiled AlphaProof Code, which formally verified the cryptographic core of Signal in four weeks.

On the consumer side, Google Wallet added digital home keys, Google Fi previewed a dual-carrier "super network", and reports suggest Grand Theft Auto VI has passed $1 billion in sales ahead of its 19 November release, a figure not yet confirmed by Take-Two. Regulators also acted: New York forced T-Mobile to drop data caps on low-income home internet plans, and Germany reportedly banned Chinese drones from military bases.

Fashion.title: Burberry rebounds as Capri names new CEO
Fashion.notification: Burberry swings back to profit as Capri names a new chief executive and luxury looks for growth beyond China.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story in fashion and luxury today is the Nvidia governance shock, though it sits at the edge of the sector, not inside it. Reports say chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after claims of extramarital relationships, one with a suspected Chinese agent, and Nvidia shares fell more than 11%. Within luxury, the clearest good news came from Burberry, which swung back to a £54m first-half profit on 6% revenue growth, with wholesale up 17% and the Americas up 12%.

Leadership change is a theme across the sector. Capri has named Estée Lauder veteran Justin Boxford as chief executive from 4 January, ending John Idol's long run, while Tod's has parted ways with creative director Matteo Tamburini. Burberry's Daniel Lee profile and Zimmermann's expansion plans add to the picture of brands leaning on creative direction and new markets.

Demand is the underlying worry. Luxury groups are reportedly turning to the United States as the Chinese growth engine stalls, and Gulf shoppers are cutting back as war-linked inflation bites. Coach and Ralph Lauren are reportedly bucking China's slump, while On Holding posted record sales and margins, helped by tariff refunds.

Tech.title: Nvidia turmoil deepens as Huang faces Congress
Tech.notification: Huang agrees to testify before Congress as pressure mounts on Commerce Secretary Lutnick over chip curbs.
Tech.summary:
The biggest story in tech right now is the fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia chief executive. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast says, with the appearance expected before Thanksgiving. Lawmakers are also focusing on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is reportedly accused of stalling tighter AI chip export curbs. Nvidia has lost about $550bn in market value in five days, and Singapore has barred Alice Huang from re-entry.

Beyond Nvidia, the wider AI trade is under pressure. Tech stocks fell sharply, with Micron and Samsung and SK Hynix hit hard, while the Anthropic IPO, priced at up to about $1.4tn, is set to be one of the largest listings ever. Attention now turns to Nvidia's results on Tuesday and the Anthropic pricing on 18 November.

Elsewhere, Microsoft said its 365 outage was fully resolved after more than a day of disruption, and SpaceX caught a Starship upper stage with its launch tower arms, a new milestone. Vulcan's failure on its first Amazon Leo launch is a setback for a rival to Starlink.

Finance.title: Rate-hike bets build as dollar hits 19-month high
Finance.notification: Fed hike bets build as the dollar hits a 19-month high, and Nvidia's earnings loom
Finance.summary:
The biggest market story is the tightening turn in US rates. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a half-point rise may be needed in December if October core inflation runs around 0.3% or higher, and the dollar climbed to a 19-month high above 101.70. Futures were already pricing a quarter-point increase at the 9 December meeting, and the 10-year Treasury yield sits above 5%. October CPI is due today, so the data will decide how far the hawkish repricing goes.

Energy is feeding that shift. Brent is near $94 to $96 after the Gulf conflict cut through Hormuz flows, and Rabobank warns of a new wave of food inflation. In the UK, traders are adding to Bank of England hike bets ahead of inflation data, and gilt yields near 4.6% have prompted mortgage repricing. Nvidia's first results since Jensen Huang's resignation are due on 17 November, and the chip sell-off has spread across Asian markets.

Deals and corporate news are lighter. Europe ended its best week since June, with banks leading, while the UK's Newmark Security takeover fight and Coca-Cola HBC's JSE listing show dealmaking still moving.

World.title: Nvidia chief quits; US, Iran and Ukraine talks in focus
World.notification: Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigns as chief executive, wiping hundreds of billions off the chipmaker's value.
World.summary:
The biggest new story in the world news feed is the resignation of Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, after revelations of two extramarital affairs, one reportedly with an alleged Chinese spy. Colette Kress has become interim chief executive, and about $500bn has reportedly been wiped off the chipmaker's value in under a week. Analysts suggest his opposition to tighter chip export controls to China may have mattered as much as the affairs, which links the story to Washington's China policy and to the wider AI trade.

Geopolitics dominates the rest of the day. Washington is reportedly warning Gulf allies that hostilities with Iran could resume as soon as Wednesday, the day after the US midterms, while the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi seizure of Bab al-Mandab keep oil and shipping risks high. A Trump-Xi-Putin meeting in Shenzhen on 19 November, alongside Europe's new five-nation negotiating group for Ukraine, adds to the diplomatic pressure.

The FAA's nationwide ground stop, now a days-old story, continues to affect airline shares and the White House push for air traffic control funding.

Fashion.title: Luxury Q3 slowdown deepens as China weighs on sector
Fashion.notification: Luxury's Q3 disappointed as China slowed further, with Kering shares down 17% in a single session.
Fashion.summary:
Luxury's third-quarter 2026 results disappointed as China's slowdown deepened. Goldman Sachs puts sector average organic sales growth at 4%, down from 7.8% in the second quarter. Kering shares plunged 17% after organic growth slowed to 1%, with Gucci down 6%, while Kering and LVMH are each down 37% year to date and Hermès is off 36%. Richemont's jewellery maisons such as Cartier slowed to 14% growth from 24%.

Analysts see the third quarter as the likely trough, but expect China to stay tough for the next two or three quarters, which keeps investors cautious. The sector's headline weakness sits alongside a governance and supply-chain problem: Loro Piana, the LVMH-owned cashmere house, has been placed under 12-month court administration over alleged worker exploitation at a Milan subcontractor. It is the fifth Italian fashion house under court monitoring since 2023, which deepens scrutiny of the Made in Italy label.

Beyond the numbers, houses are widening their reach. Dior is backing women filmmakers with Sundance, Guerlain is opening its largest spa at the Bellagio in Las Vegas, and Estée Lauder has opened a joint travel-retail store in Miami with Duty Free Americas.
